name: Carla Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and fit timber acoustic partitions on building sites, currently in a community centre. My vocational trade certificate started me off, and I'm an experienced fitter on a higher wage because I take evening work, not because I run the site. I like a quiet room after we seal the joints; late boards can waste a whole night.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner delivers for a bakery, our children are grown, and we have about eight months of expenses saved. There are plenty of similar builders nearby. I use AI now and then to read product sheets; I also go to our builders' union meetings, and I hope to leave regular site work around 65 if our retirement figures cover the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a quicker timber list is welcome, but somebody still has to keep the acoustic wall straight. I would ask the builder to spend any saved office time on proper paid fitting time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm on a higher carpenter wage because I take evening acoustic-partition jobs, but I am not the foreman. My partner's bakery-delivery income and eight months of expenses saved make this mild change easy to absorb while we check whether retirement at 65 is affordable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting the community centre partitions and check each stud against the room marks. At the next union meeting I'll bring the contractor's recent shortened-shift notices and ask for a minimum paid callout when evening materials arrive late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and money this year. The retirement check is a household chore, not a reason to leave a paid site job today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When did the partition drawing miss something?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last Thursday the drawing showed a stud where a ventilation duct now passes. We moved the community centre wall stud before closing it and checked the sound seal again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you take to the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the dated delivery notice and the hours actually paid for that evening. The union representative could then ask for a written minimum rather than a vague promise.

say: **Acoustic walls** still need measured studs and sound seals after routine paperwork improves.
Builders should preserve **paid fitting time** when office lists speed up.
think: My **evening-site premium** and partner's wages support the household.
Eight months of **saved expenses** give us room to assess retirement at 65.
do: **Fit** community centre partitions and check studs against room marks.
**Bring** late-delivery shift notices to union meeting for minimum paid callout.
feel: **Calm** about current work, reviewing retirement only for planning.
S0.quote: We moved the community centre wall stud before closing it and checked the sound seal again.
fieldNote: She corrects a **duct conflict** by checking the real partition before closing it, rather than trusting a drawing.
Her **union request** concerns a documented minimum paid evening callout; strong savings support present calm.

steps.text: Fit community centre partitions and check studs against room marks
Bring dated delivery notices to union meeting for paid callout

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI may order boards and write the inspection notes before robots fit acoustic partitions. I will accept a new screen once a wall crew has shown it works on a real room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own evening fitting hours look safe in the near term, but an office order that misses a duct can waste a paid night. I have savings and plenty of local builders, so I can insist on a check without fearing next week's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll compare two office board lists with the measured community centre rooms. If the new AI ordering screen is adopted, another fitter demonstrates its corrections on a finished room and paid practice time is offered, I'll learn its edit controls before the next live order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about a rushed order, though my own wage looks secure. I have no need to be the first person to touch every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you stop a wrong board order?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would mark the duct on the plan and call the yard before boards are cut. An acoustic wall cannot swallow a ventilation duct just because the order sheet is tidy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why insist on a finished-room demonstration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A finished room gives us the real board lengths and duct clearance to compare. If the screen misses either, I would send hand-marked measurements until the controls have been fixed.

say: **AI ordering** changes office lists before robots fit partitions.
A fitter should test **duct clearances** before a board order is final.
think: My own **evening wage** still looks secure.
Wrong **board lengths** could waste a shift, cushioned by savings and plentiful nearby builders.
do: **Compare** two board lists with measured community centre rooms.
**Learn** adopted AI edits on paid time after fitter proves finished-room corrections.
feel: **Uneasy** about bad orders, with income secure for now.
S1.quote: An acoustic wall cannot swallow a ventilation duct just because the order sheet is tidy.
fieldNote: She learns **new AI controls** only after an adopted screen is proven on a finished room with paid practice time.
Her concern is **wasted work time**, not a stated likelihood of her own wage disappearing in this slower change.

steps.text: Compare two board lists with measured community centre rooms
Learn adopted AI edits on paid time after finished-room demonstration

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking AI by 2028 could design the partitions, and capable robots around 2031 could fit them. Workers should see the paid crew plan before a robot demonstration is booked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 63 when robots can do the physical fitting, two years before the age I hope to stop if our figures allow. A lost evening partition premium could leave a retirement gap despite eight months saved and many local contractors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the workplace union to request written partition crew numbers and a paid safe robot trial. My partner and I will review retirement income against bills; if the firm cuts my paid nights, I'll apply only to posted local acoustic-fit or inspection jobs with safe hours and pay sufficient for those bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the premium before retirement is affordable, while savings and local work give us options. I am not booking an early exit from a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your grown children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our grown children we are checking the figures ourselves before any work decision. They have their own households and I don't want a missing site wage to become their bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a safe robot trial need to show?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The robot should fit a full corner with a real duct and a worker able to stop the machine. A flat showroom wall would not show the clash that delayed our site last week.

say: **2028 thinking AI** designs partitions before robots fit them around 2031.
Workers need **paid crew numbers** and a safe site trial.
think: At about **63**, a lost evening premium could create a retirement gap.
Eight months of **savings** and nearby builders give options, not guaranteed income to 65.
do: **Ask** workplace union for partition crew numbers and paid safe trial.
**Review** retirement statements against household bills with partner.
**Apply** after night cuts to posted local acoustic job with safe bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible wage gap before planned retirement.
S2.quote: A lost evening partition premium could leave a retirement gap despite eight months saved and many local contractors.
fieldNote: She may still need the **evening wage** at 63, before her hoped-for exit at 65.
Applications require **actual shift cuts** and a posted local role with safe hours and household bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Ask workplace union for partition crew numbers and paid safe trial
Review retirement statements against household bills with partner
Apply after night cuts to posted local acoustic job with safe bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2031 could draft the partition plan, then robots around 2034 could build it. Five years should buy time for a paid inspection course and a real wall test, if the contractor will sign the terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 66 when robots can fit walls, a year after I hope to leave regular sites. If our retirement income covers the bills, I may already be off the rota; if it falls short, the evening wage could still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner and I will check retirement statements and bills each year. I'll ask the contractor to fund a recognised acoustic-inspection course with paid class time and a real place; if those terms are agreed, I'll enrol, then apply after any shift cut only to posted local inspection jobs with safe hours and pay that covers our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the possibility that retirement figures fall short, though the extra years let us get terms in writing. I will not give up a paid construction night for an acoustic-inspection course flyer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a useful wall test measure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want the robot trial to measure the sound seal around a real duct and record who signs it off. A straight test wall would not show whether the corner leaks noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the course more than a briefing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The course must include site assessment, paid class hours and fees covered. If the contractor will only invite me to a briefing, I will keep working and checking real vacancies.

say: **2031 thinking AI** drafts plans before robots build partitions around 2034.
A **duct-corner test** and paid inspection course need written terms.
think: At about **66**, affordable retirement may already have taken me off site.
If income falls short, the **evening wage** may still be needed.
do: **Review** retirement statements against bills with partner yearly.
**Enrol** in recognised acoustic-inspection course if fees, real place and paid class time secured.
**Apply** after qualification, cuts and income shortfall to posted local inspection job with safe bill-covering pay.
feel: **Anxious** about uncertain retirement income, with time to seek terms.
S3.quote: I will not give up a paid construction night for an acoustic-inspection course flyer.
fieldNote: Her hoped-for exit at **65 is conditional** on actual income, so a robot at 66 could still threaten wages.
Training needs **funded fees**, paid time and a real place; later applications require posted local work with safe bill-covering pay.

steps.text: Review retirement statements against bills with partner yearly
Enrol in recognised acoustic-inspection course if fees, place and paid class time secured
Apply after qualification, cuts and income shortfall to posted local inspection job with safe bill-covering pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI by 2036 may draw walls and capable robots around 2039 may fit them. I hope to have left regular site work around 65 if our income can carry us, and the next crew should get paid time to learn sound-seal checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be about 71 when robots do the physical fitting, well past my hoped-for exit. Our eight-month reserve makes planning easier, but I still want actual retirement figures before treating that exit as settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep fitting partitions on the current rota and review retirement statements with my partner each year. At the builders' union training group I'll propose paid apprentice time on real duct corners, then walk a younger fitter through one finished wall before I leave if our figures support retiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the final retirement number, though the robot date itself is far beyond my hoped-for work. I can pass on the tricky part without pretending I will be on site in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you show a younger fitter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put a light behind the duct corner and show the younger fitter where the seal breaks. A robot's perfect wall drawing will not keep noise out of a real classroom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the union training request concrete?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The training request would name paid apprentice hours, a working wall and the person who signs off the seal. Our union group could put that to the builder before I stop regular shifts.

say: **2036 thinking AI** plans walls before robots fit them around 2039.
**Paid apprentice checks** can preserve acoustic fitting skill after older workers leave.
think: At about **71**, robots arrive beyond my hoped-for regular work.
Retirement at **65 still depends** on statements that cover bills.
do: **Keep** fitting partitions on current site rota.
**Review** retirement statements with partner each year.
**Propose** paid duct-corner practice at builders' union training group.
feel: **Uneasy** about retirement affordability, with a long handover window.
S4.quote: A robot's perfect wall drawing will not keep noise out of a real classroom.
fieldNote: She separates **today's paid site work** from a conditional handover before retirement, never asserting employment at 71.
Her union proposal names **paid apprentice hours**, a real duct corner and a sign-off worker, fitting her progressive view.

steps.text: Keep fitting partitions on current site rota
Review retirement statements with partner yearly
Propose paid duct-corner practice at builders union training group

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could cut evening fitting pay when I would be about 63, before my hoped-for exit. A written crew plan, paid safe trial and actual local jobs with adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the sound seal after a robot finishes a wall beside a classroom duct. A partition can look smooth and still let every word travel through the corner. Someone must test it before handover.

headlineQuote: A partition can look smooth and still let every word travel through the corner.
portrait: **Carla**, 58, is an experienced acoustic partition fitter with a vocational certificate and higher pay from evening site shifts.
Her bakery-delivery partner and grown children share an **eight-month reserve**; plentiful nearby builders offer alternatives.
She uses **AI occasionally**, trusts a proven site tool and raises paid training and callout terms through the builders' union.
Fast robots make her **anxious** about a wage gap before a conditional exit around 65; slow change supports a paid handover.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring partition robots around 2031, when she would be about 63 and still need evening pay.
whatWouldHelp: A **written crew plan**, paid safe trial and real local roles with adequate pay would support a careful transition.
